tracks.title: The engine you own
tracks.text: Lesson two — the Nexus. The Nexus runs workbooks… on your laptop, your server, or your cloud account. And docking is what turns a file into living software. Isolated… stateful… agentic. [curious] This lesson is about why you'd want to own the engine… and how one machine carries you from first prototype, all the way to production.

tracks.title: Where does your software live?
tracks.text: [curious] Where does your software live… when you're not looking? Almost everything you own digitally runs on a computer that isn't yours. Your notes… your photos… the app your business depends on. They live in someone's datacenter — and what you actually own is a login. That trade has real upsides. But notice what it does to software you build. Your own creation lives somewhere you can't see… priced per request… on terms that change under you. [sighs] And the agent era sharpened this from a philosophical itch… into a bill. Agents need a computer to live on. The industry's answer has been to rent that computer in slices — a fresh micro virtual machine per agent, metered by the second. At prototype scale, it feels free. Then you scale… and the meter is the business model. [chuckles] People have resorted to parking Mac minis in closets, just to give an agent somewhere permanent to exist. Which tells you the demand is real — even when the answer is silly. [excited] The missing piece isn't a cheaper rental. It's an engine you own.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. The Nexus is the engine that runs workbooks. You run it — on a laptop, a server, or your own cloud account. And docking a workbook into it is what makes the file isolated… stateful… and agentic. It's called Nexus because that's its job. The point where your workbooks, your data, your services, and your agents connect. The one piece of the system that's a place… rather than a file. A workbook is the thing you hand to anyone. The Nexus is the thing you plug it into.

tracks.title: What docking actually means
tracks.text: [curious] So what does docking actually mean? On its own, a workbook is an artifact. Complete… portable… and inert while it's closed. Dock it into a Nexus, and three things switch on. First — isolated. The workbook runs in its own sealed compartment. It can't reach the host machine, your keychain, or any other workbook. It gets exactly the capabilities you grant it. Second — stateful. Its database becomes live, persistent, and synced. Schedules fire overnight… state survives restarts. And third — agentic. Agents attached to the workbook get somewhere permanent to live and work… with their files and memory in the workbook they're tending. [excited] And here's the part I love. It's the same file, before and after. Nothing was converted, exported, or deployed in the traditional sense. File in… living software out.

tracks.title: Built on a boring miracle
tracks.text: Here's the part most platforms bury in a footnote — told up front, because it's the best reason to trust the design. The Nexus is built on the BEAM… the virtual machine behind Erlang. Not new. Not trendy. Not experimental. It was engineered by Ericsson to run telephone exchanges. Millions of simultaneous calls… every call isolated from every other call. The famous figure is nine nines of uptime. [chuckles] That's about thirty-one milliseconds of downtime… per year. And the design that achieves it is almost insultingly simple. Everything is a tiny, isolated process. If one crashes, it takes nothing down with it. A supervisor notices… and replaces it, mid-flight. [excited] The Nexus inherits that whole posture for free. Every docked workbook, every agent, every request… is one of those processes. A workbook crashing is a non-event. And that's why one modest machine goes so far. The BEAM was built to hold millions of concurrent processes. Thousands of workbooks on one server isn't a stretch goal… it's the VM's home turf.

tracks.title: Isolation, twice
tracks.text: Depth rung — the mechanism behind the isolated light. BEAM processes isolate workbooks from each other. But a workbook also carries arbitrary code… its WebAssembly could have been written by anyone. So that code runs inside a second wall. A WebAssembly sandbox — the same engine class browsers trust. Code gets memory it can't escape… and only the capabilities explicitly handed in. Grants — not inheritance. So the nesting goes… machine… engine… process… sandbox. Code would have to break out of two unrelated containment systems, just to reach its neighbor. [curious] And one detail that says a lot about the philosophy. Even the compilers live inside the sandbox. When the Nexus builds code, the compiler itself has been compiled to WebAssembly… and runs under the same containment. Nothing untrusted ever executes natively on the host. [whispers] Not even the toolchain.

tracks.title: Why not serverless? Why not rent?
tracks.text: [curious] Why not serverless? Why not rent the VMs? Because of what agents and living software actually are. Serverless functions are built for ephemeral work. A request comes in… a function spins up… answers… and evaporates. Nothing about an agent is ephemeral. An agent is a long-running thing — with memory, files, schedules. The precise opposite of the serverless shape. [sighs] You can duct-tape persistence onto function calls — and people do. But you're fighting the model… and the meter is still running while you fight it. Rented sandboxes fix the shape problem, but keep the meter. You're paying for isolation as a service… by the second… forever. The Nexus's answer — isolation is software, not a subscription. The BEAM and the WebAssembly sandbox do what the rented VM was doing… on a machine you own. And the economics invert. One small server runs thousands of isolated workbooks, concurrently. When you outgrow it, you don't multiply line items. [excited] You grow the machine.

tracks.title: The security model, plainly
tracks.text: The security model — plainly. Start with why agent setups are scary. An agent running with operating system access is an open box. Your keychain… your environment variables… your API keys. And bad instruction is the part people underestimate. Prompt injection means anyone whose text reaches your agent — a web page it reads, an email it summarizes — is partially steering it. The Nexus's frame: never trust the workload. Structure the world so it doesn't have to be trusted. That lands as three rules. First — capabilities are granted, not inherited. A workbook starts with nothing. No network… no host files… no secrets. Each power is a specific, revocable grant. Second — secrets stay in the engine. Code in the sandbox never holds credentials… so there's nothing to leak. And third — the blast radius is one process. Compromised, or just broken, a workbook can trash exactly itself. [excited] None of this requires you to do security engineering. It's just what the architecture does.

tracks.title: Dev is prod
tracks.text: Dev is prod — one engine, every stage. The classic software journey crosses three worlds. The thing on your laptop… the staging copy… and production. Most works on my machine misery is those worlds disagreeing. [excited] There is exactly one Nexus. The engine on your laptop and the engine in your cloud are the same engine. Same image… same behavior. And a deployment is described by one declarative file. Where it runs is a value in that file. Flip local to cloud… and the prototype you built for yourself is the product your team runs. No translation layer. No re-platforming cliff. No now make it real rewrite.

tracks.title: What the Nexus isn't
tracks.text: Honesty section — what the Nexus isn't. It isn't serverless-with-extra-steps. It's a server. [chuckles] That's the point. You own a thing that runs. What ownership costs you is knowing the thing exists… what it buys you is everything above. It isn't a number-cruncher. The BEAM's genius is coordination — not raw math. Heavy computation belongs in the WebAssembly lane. The engine coordinates… the sandbox computes. Knowing which half does which is most of understanding the design. And it isn't required. Workbooks open in any browser — no engine in sight. Viewing is free… forever… by design.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Do I need a Nexus to open a workbook? No. Files open in any browser. You need one when you want a workbook to live. What does it cost to run? Whatever the machine costs — that's the whole model. A laptop runs it for free… a small VPS runs a serious multi-tenant install. Local versus cloud — what's actually different? Position… not kind. Same engine image either way. Moving between them is editing one value. Can my team share one? Yes. Multi-tenancy with organization-level isolation is built into the engine. Tenants share the machine… and never each other's data. And — I already have a database. Do I abandon it? No. SQLite is the travels-with-the-file default… not a wall.

tracks.title: Wrapping up
tracks.text: So that's the Nexus. One engine — your laptop, your server, your cloud — and docking is what turns a file into living software. [curious] Next up… the parts. What agents and workbooks actually reach for when they work. Toolkits.
